title: Starlace and the Star-Lantern's Light
markdown:
On the edge of the Whispering Woods, where the sky kisses sleepy earth, stood Whisperwind Hill, crowned with ancient grasses. Atop it shone a legend: the Star-Lantern, a crystal ball carved from one huge gem, filled with captured starlight. Its beam was a beacon for lost travelers and a signal to the Sky-Weavers, who guided the grand Cloud Parade across the heavens.

Upon that hill, on moss kissed by the moon, lived Starlace the unicorn. Her coat was moonlight-soft. Her silver mane fell like water. From her forehead grew a horn that held a bright shine and could make magic light. Yet she held a secret: she, bright Starlace, was deeply afraid of the dark. As evening painted purple and pink and the first faint stars showed, a shiver went through her sides. The Star-Lantern, usually a bloom of light, was dimming, its shine fading, long shadows dancing with every breath of wind.

From a burrow under an old oak came Tuck the mole, tireless and clever, fur the colour of rich earth, spectacles on his twitching nose. He scurried to Starlace, paws tapping dewy grass.

“Starlace,” he said, concern in his small voice. “The Star-Lantern is fading, and fast. The Great Cloud Parade visits tonight. Without the lantern’s true glow, the Sky-Weavers will lose their way. They need its steady beam.”

Starlace’s eyes, wide as twilight pools, darted to the dimming ball. Her hooves shifted. “Tuck. It is growing so dark. The shadows stretch and twist. My horn feels less bright.”

“That is why we must climb. The lantern needs its inner fire stirred. It is our duty, and our adventure.”

They began. Tuck led, keen nose on the path, pausing at roots Starlace might miss. Starlace followed, hooves careful on dew-slick grass, breath catching at every deepening shadow that seemed to stretch like fingers. The hill that was friendly by day grew taller. The air cooled: damp earth, distant pine, night flowers opening as if they had been waiting for this particular evening. A nightjar called once and was still.

Then a mighty gust roared through the tall grasses, an unseen hand, and snuffed the Star-Lantern’s last weak flicker.

Darkness fell complete. Trees and rocks vanished. Starlace gasped, a small choked sound. Her legs felt like unset jelly. Her heart pounded against her ribs. Her horn’s inner light shrank from the black. She wanted the burrow, the oak, any shape she knew. “I cannot, Tuck. The dark is too great. It feels alive.”

Tuck did not waver. A small determined shape, spectacles glinting faintly. “Think of the parade. The wonder for creatures below. The little ones who might be lost without its beam. And think of your own light, hidden but always there. Your horn holds starlight. That cannot be truly put out.”

His words were a steady hand in the overwhelming dark. She remembered the pulse beneath her fear, a thrum like a far drum. She closed her eyes, pushed the shadows back, and imagined the lantern not as a distant worry but as a promise she could help keep. A shaky breath. Another, tasting pine. She stepped forward, one hoof, then the next. “You are right. We must go on. For the parade, and for ourselves.”

They pressed on, quicker now, the hill’s crest a rumour of crystal. At the lantern’s base the orb stood a silent husk, former glory only a memory, cold to the muzzle. The stone pedestal, polished smooth by ages, where the magic dewdrop usually rested, was bare. Empty. In the distance a soft glow began to paint the sky: the first wisps of the Cloud Parade, magnificent ships of vapour, and time alarmingly short.

Panic tightened. The dewdrop gone, darkness still heavy, whispering doubts. Then a memory flickered, faint as a distant echo: a hidden grove deep in the woods, known only to a few, where moonpetal flowers bloomed. Their petals, delicate as spun moonlight, unfurled at nightfall and held tiny beads of dew that shone with captured starlight. She had been there once in kinder dusk, when Tuck was not even with her, and had been too shy of the dark to stay.

“The moonpetals. They hold dew born of the moon.” She lowered her horn, not with fear now but purpose. Starlight cut a gentle path through the undergrowth. “Follow me, Tuck. Quickly.”

They raced. Starlace’s horn was a guiding star, lighting a winding trail through ancient trunks that had seen many parades and many fears. Tuck scampered behind, spectacles catching the clear light, paws sure on roots. An owl watched and did not comment. The grove opened at last, pale blooms unfurling as they arrived, each shimmering with a silvery inner shine that pushed at the shadows. Dew sat on the petals like tiny held moons. Carefully, touch as gentle as a sigh, Starlace nudged the flowers and gathered the radiant dew into a single drop that pulsed warm in her hoof, heavier than it looked, as if starlight had weight.

They turned and ran, lungs burning, the parade a symphony of celestial whispers ahead, closer now, clouds like ships looking for a harbour. Wind on Whisperwind Hill seemed to change sides and cheer. At the pedestal Starlace hesitated only long enough to be sure her hoof would not shake. Then, fear conquered for this night, she placed the moonpetal dewdrop where the old one should have been.

A soft hum. A pulse through the crystal, energy spreading like dawn inside a gem. The Star-Lantern blazed, starlight filling the night, a beacon of wonder for anyone still on a path. The Cloud Parade drifted serenely, sculpted clouds and celestial art guided by that steady beam. Starlace stood tall in the magnificent light. The dark was still there, beyond the hill’s rim, in the woods they had run through. It did not own her horn. Tuck adjusted his spectacles and watched the parade, a small mole on a high place, while Starlace’s silver mane lifted in the same wind that had tried to put the lantern out, and failed. Below, some traveler on a lane would see the hill bloom and know the way. That was enough. That was the adventure, finished and beginning at once.
